description: Third batch of raw journal entries. The bunker enters its second winter. Stored food is declining, greenhouse production is rising, fuel is the bottleneck. New voices join the record; returning voices show how the months have changed them. Covers Days 115 through 162.

entries.text: The crossover point I projected at Day 100 has not arrived. It will not arrive this month. Greenhouse production is up to eleven percent of caloric need, which sounds like progress until you do the arithmetic: eleven percent of forty-seven people is five point one seven people. We are feeding five people from the greenhouse and slowly starving the other forty-two from the stores. The rice is at thirty-eight kilos. I have stopped writing the days-supply number on the board because the number makes people quiet in a way I do not like. The Chef asked me this morning what the plan is. I told her the plan is to plant more turnips. She did not laugh. She said turnips are not a plan. I know they are not a plan. They are a vegetable.

The feed line to the cistern froze last night at the elbow where it comes through the foundation wall. I have been telling the Architect since Day 90 that the insulation on that elbow is insufficient. She said there was no insulation left. There is no insulation left. So I wrapped it in three layers of salvaged blanket and a sheet of the rubber pond liner the Botanist was using for the mushroom trays. She was not happy about the pond liner. I was not happy about the freeze. The line thawed by midday with a hot-water pour. If it had cracked we would have lost the cistern feed and been on bucket duty from the lower sump. That is eight flights of stairs per bucket. I do not want to think about it. I am going to find insulation. I do not know where. I am going to find it.

I have begun keeping the list. Not the list of the dead — the Undertaker keeps that, and he is meticulous. My list is of the living, with the day each person arrived and the thing they said first when they came through the airlock. Some of them said nothing. I write 'silence' for those. Some of them said a name that was not their own — a child's name, a wife's name, a city. I write what they said. The list is forty-seven entries long now. I read it sometimes when the bunker feels empty in a way that has nothing to do with the number of people in it. Forty-seven is not empty. Forty-seven is a great deal. But the list reminds me that each of the forty-seven was once a single person standing in an airlock, and someone wrote down what they said. That was me. I am the only one who heard all of them.

Built a hand crane today from the front axle of a tractor and two lengths of the stainless pipe the Mechanic's team brought back from the geo-thermal plant. It lifts the generator fuel drums off the floor so we can roll them instead of dragging them. Dragging was bending the floor plates under the drum cradles. The General came down to look at it and said it was the most useful thing built in the bunker this month. I told him the Botanist built a wheat plant this month. He said wheat plants do not move drums. He is right. The crane does not move drums either, technically. It lifts them. Rolling is what the person does. I am being precise because the General is not precise and someone in this bunker should be.

I moved back to the dormitory on Day 122. The Therapist did not ask me to. I moved because the laundry alcove began to smell like me, and I did not want to become a person who smells like a laundry alcove. The dormitory is loud. People breathe in their sleep. Some of them talk. The Bouncer calls out a name I do not recognise. The Exhausted Father's daughter coughs in the small hours — a dry cough, the Surgeon says it is dust, not sickness, but I listen for it now. I have learned the breathing of seven people. I did not want to learn it. But it is the sound of the bunker being full, and a full bunker is a thing I am trying to be grateful for. The towels are still in the alcove. I did not move the towels. I go and fold them sometimes. It is not a nest anymore. It is a place I used to be.

Second batch of potassium iodide tablets is curing in the drying cabinet. The first batch held its shape for nineteen days before the bark binder began to crumble. I adjusted the ratio — less bark, more of the starch the Chef saved from the potato peelings she has been dehydrating. The starch binds better but the tablets take longer to dry. Four days instead of two. The Pharmacist says shelf life should improve to thirty days. I will believe it when I see it. We have enough potassium iodide stock for perhaps four more batches. After that we need a new source of potassium. The Historian says there is a pre-war agricultural supply depot marked on the Cartographer's map, twelve kilometres northwest. I have not told the General yet. I am waiting until I am certain the tablets work, so that when I ask for the expedition I can say what we are going for and why it matters. A reason is a thing that makes an expedition into something other than a risk.

the Teacher gave me a pencil today that is only mine. It has my name on it on a piece of tape. She said a pencil that is only yours means you can write whenever you want and no one can take it. I wrote my name in the book. I wrote it four times because I wanted to see it. Then I wrote the word for water because that is the first word she taught me. Then I closed the book. I do not want to write the other things. The pencil is yellow. It is the only yellow thing in the bunker. I keep it in my sock so it does not get taken. the Teacher said no one will take it. I keep it in my sock anyway.

Brownout at 02:40. Voltage dropped to 198 for eleven minutes. The medical bay cold storage alarmed. The Surgeon came down in his coat and stood behind me while I worked. He did not say anything. He did not need to say anything. The voltage regulator bypass I wired at Day 43 is failing on three more channels. I have one channel left. After that the generator runs unregulated and the voltage will swing with load. I shut down the greenhouse grow lights and the radio standby and the lower corridor heaters and held the medical bay and the ventilation alone. The voltage came back to 214. The Surgeon left without speaking. I sat with the generator until dawn. At 06:00 I turned the grow lights back on. The Botanist will be angry. The plants do not know about brownouts. I will explain it to the plants and to the Botanist and one of them will understand.

No one came to the chapel this week. Not for the Wednesday gathering, not for the Sunday quiet hour. The chapel is a store room we cleared of crates and filled with six folding chairs and a table I call an altar because it is the table we put things on when we need a table to put things on. I do not have a book. I had a book. It was water-damaged and the pages stuck and I could not turn them without tearing. I tore out the pages I could still read and I read them until I had read them and then I had nothing left to read. I speak now from what I remember. I am not certain I remember it correctly. The Watchmaker says memory is a mechanism that drifts and must be calibrated against an external standard. I do not have an external standard. I have what I remember. I sat in the chapel alone for an hour. Six chairs and a table and one person who remembers. That is enough for a chapel. It has to be.

The wolves came back. Three days ago the tracks were gone and I told the Cop the pack had moved north after the deer. I was wrong. They moved east to the ridge and they have come back with more. Nine animals now. I counted the prints in the snow at the frozen river approach. Nine. The Courier and I went to the barge cache for what we thought would be the last meat before thaw and the wolves were on the far bank watching us. They did not come across. They watched. A wolf that watches is learning. A wolf that learns where the food is and where the people are becomes a different kind of problem. I fired a warning shot. They did not move. They watched the shot hit the ice and they did not move. I do not like this. I told the General. He said carry the rifle on all river missions. I said I already do. He said carry two. I do not have two.

I opened the microphone at 18:00 and nothing came out. Not static. Not silence. Nothing. I sat with my hand on the switch and my mouth open and the words were not there. The broadcast was supposed to be the evening address and the water update and a request from the Watchmaker for a small mainspring if anyone has one. I could not say any of it. I sat for what I think was a minute. It may have been longer. Then I said, 'This is the bunker radio. The evening broadcast will be delayed. Stay where you are.' I do not know why I said stay where you are. People are already where they are. I turned off the transmitter. I went to the Therapist. She was not there. I went to the chapel. The Priest was there alone. I sat in one of the six chairs. He did not speak. We sat. After a while he said, 'You do not have to have words.' I went back to the transmitter at 19:30 and did the broadcast. The words were there the second time. I do not know where they had gone.

The wheat named for Tomas has set seed. Four heads. I cut them today with the small scissors the Watchmaker lent me and I held them in my hand and I counted the grains. Thirty-one grains. Thirty-one grains from one seed is not a harvest. It is a proof. It is proof that wheat will grow here and will seed here and that the seed will be true. I will plant all thirty-one. If even half take, I will have one hundred and fifty grains next cycle, and after that, enough to try a small outdoor plot when the Meteorologist says the surface dose has dropped. She says maybe by Day 200. Maybe. I put the four seed heads in the envelope with the letter to Tomas. I did not seal it. I want him to see them. I know he cannot see them. I put them in the envelope anyway. The third seedling from the left was always the strongest. I told Galina. She said she would make sure no one moved the envelope. She did not ask why I was crying. She is good at not asking why.

The vote was not unanimous. I want to write that down because I do not want to forget it and I do not want to pretend it was easy. Six for, one against, two abstentions. The Electrician voted against. He said he was not voting against children. He said he was voting for the generator. He is right. The generator is the thing that keeps the children in this bunker alive, and the generator runs on fuel, and the fuel is at 15 days, and 15 days is the number I see when I close my eyes. The Surgeon abstained. The Architect abstained. They could not rank the three and they chose not to pretend. That is honest. I respect honest more than I respect agreement. The Therapist watched me during the vote. She has a session with me on Day 172. I think she was watching to see if I would carry it. I will carry it. That is what a general is for. A general is the person who decides and then does not get to put the decision down. The Courier said: if we go, I will go. If we do not go, I will listen for them until the radio stops. He is 22 years old. He should not have to say that. No one should have to say that. But he said it, and he meant it, and the room was quiet after he said it, and the quiet was the thing that decided. Not me. The quiet. I gave the order. The team leaves Day 167. The Courier, the Hunter, the Plumber, the Quartermaster. Four people and 80 litres of water and 56 kilometres of walking and a well that is dry. The Priest said a prayer after the vote. No one joined him. He said it anyway. I did not bow my head. I am not a man who bows his head. But I heard it. I heard all of it. The prayer was not for Kilo. The prayer was for us. I think the Priest knows that. I think the Priest has known that since the chapel emptied. I will address the bunker on Day 171 when the team is back. I do not know what I will say. I know what I will not say. I will not say it was the right decision. I do not know if it was the right decision. I know it was the decision. That is all a general gets to know.

They are back. I stood at the airlock at 22:00. I did not plan to stand at the airlock. I was going to stand in the corridor. I stood at the airlock. The Quartermaster came through first. He looked at me and said, 'Twelve people who will live.' I did not say anything. The Plumber came through carrying nothing — he had left his tools. He said the well is a three-day dig and they will do it themselves. The Hunter came through with the rifle and did not speak. He nodded. That is the Hunter. The Courier came through last. He was carrying the empty water containers, which is wrong, because the containers should have been left. I asked him why he brought them back. He said, 'They gave them back. They washed them.' He said the man with the radio put the radio down to dig. I did not understand. He explained. The man had been holding the radio for 16 days, waiting for an answer. When the answer came, he put the radio down and picked up a shovel. I stood in the airlock for a while after they had gone to the mess hall. The airlock smelled of cold and four people and 56 kilometres. I addressed the bunker at 22:30. I said: 'The team is back. The mission is done. Twelve people have water. We did not lose anything we cannot replace.' I did not say the rest. The rest is that we did not lose anything we cannot replace because the Courier and the Hunter and the Plumber and the Quartermaster walked 56 kilometres and did not get hurt, and that is luck, and luck is not a plan. I will see the Therapist on Day 172. I will tell her about the quiet in the room after the Courier spoke. I have not told anyone about the quiet. I am writing it here because the page does not ask me to explain it. The quiet was the sound of a room full of people deciding to be the kind of people who go. I do not know if we are those people. We went. That has to be enough.

Two meetings today. The Therapist at 14:00. The council at 18:00. I will write about the council because the council is the thing that will not let me sleep, and I will write about the Therapist because she is the reason I might. The Therapist knew about the quiet. I did not tell her. The Historian told her. I did not know the Historian reads the journals. I do not know if I am angry about this. I think I am not. The Historian is the bunker's memory and the memory spoke before I did, which is what memories do. The Therapist said the sessions do not have a goal and do not have an end date. I said good. I almost smiled. I did not smile. The almost is the thing I am holding onto tonight. The council was the harder meeting. Fuel at 17 days. Antibiotics at zero. We argued the order. The Electrician wants fuel first. The Surgeon wants antibiotics first. I broke it: fuel first, antibiotics second, because a dead generator makes the antibiotic run a suicide mission. The Surgeon abstained. The Priest abstained. The Priest said he could not rank fuel above medicine and could not rank medicine above fuel. I understand. I do not agree. Understanding and agreeing are different and the council needs both. I said after the vote: we are not choosing between fuel and antibiotics. We are choosing the order in which we fail at both, and hoping we do not fail at either. I do not know if that is true. I know it is the kind of thing a general says. The Hunter asked about the rifles after the meeting. He has one. I told him to carry two. He said he has one. I said I know. I did not resolve it. I do not have a second rifle. I have a vote and an order and 17 days of fuel and zero antibiotics and one rifle and 47 people who are sleeping because they do not know the number I see when I close my eyes. I will see the Therapist on Day 179. I will come because I said I would come. That is the only commitment I have made this week that I am certain I can keep. The rest is the order: fuel, then antibiotics, then whatever comes after, if anything does.

The diesel is dirty and it is recoverable. I spent the day with a jar of frozen diesel pool and a set of filters and a Watchmaker's heated plate and I can say with the certainty of a person who has done the test: the train yard pool will yield 11 to 19 litres of generator-grade diesel after filtration through cloth, sand, and the greenhouse fleece the Botanist will not be happy about losing. The locomotive tank, if the Veteran is right about the siphon residue, holds another 20 litres below the draw pipe. 30 to 45 litres. 3 to 4 days of generator runtime. The council ordered the fuel expedition first. I told them the yield is a breath, not a solution. They ordered it anyway. A breath is what we have. I have written the filtration procedure for the Mechanic. He is a good hand and he will follow it. I have written the contamination screen for myself because I am the one who stays. I am not going. I told the General this and he did not ask why. I think he knows. The lab is the place where I am most useful and the field is the place where I am least useful. A Chemist in the field is a person with a jar and a fear of the open. I have the fear. I have had it since before. The fear is not about the radiation. The fear is about the sky. I do not say this to the Therapist. I do not say this to anyone. I am writing it here because the page does not ask me to be brave. The page asks me to be accurate. The accurate thing is: the diesel is recoverable, the yield is a breath, and the Chemist is not going. The Veteran leads. The Mechanic filters. The Courier carries. The Hunter watches. They go on Day 178. I will be in the lab. I will be waiting for the reference sample. The reference sample is the unfiltered diesel, and I will compare it to the filtered fraction and I will know if the filtration worked. That is my work. The field is theirs. The breath is everyone's.

I wrote the list today. I wrote it with a pen that was running dry because I could not find a pen that was not running dry and the list could not wait. Amoxicillin. Doxycycline. Ciprofloxacin. Metronidazole. Suture material, non-absorbable, 3-0 and 4-0. IV fluids, lactated Ringer's if it exists. Analgesics, anything. Antiseptic, chlorhexidine preferred. I wrote the storage conditions: sealed manufacturer packaging, cool, dry, out of direct light. I wrote the expiry guidance: most antibiotics 12 to 24 months past expiry if stored correctly. I wrote it for the Courier, who is 22 and is not a pharmacist and is not a surgeon and is going to walk 14 kilometres to a warehouse that may be empty or hot or both and try to find the thing that stands between this bunker and the next infection. I spent 40 minutes with him. I showed him what the packaging looks like. I showed him the difference between a blister pack and a bottle and a vial. I told him the names. He repeated them. He wrote them on his hand because the laminated list might be lost and his hand is harder to lose. His hands are young and steady. My hands shook. He did not mention it. I am grateful he did not mention it. I did not volunteer for the expedition. I told the Therapist it was the single-provider logic. It is the single-provider logic. It is also the fact that I cannot be the man who walks into the warehouse and finds it empty. I can be the man who waits in the clinic and hears it was empty. I do not know which is worse. I know which one I chose. The list is written. The Courier has it. The team leaves Day 183. I will be in the clinic. I will be waiting. The waiting is the part of medicine they do not teach you, because it cannot be taught. It can only be done.

We go southwest tomorrow. I do not know the southwest. I know the east — the river, the wolves, the deer, the ridge. The southwest is the Cartographer's map and the Veteran's route and nothing else. The wolves are an east pack. I told the General they may not be southwest. He said may. May is the word that makes me carry the rifle and the flares and not sleep on the return. I have not slept on a return since the river. The Courier says I will sleep when we are back. I told him I sleep when the bunker door is closed. He said that is not sleep, that is relief. He is 22 and he knows the difference. I did not know the difference at 22. The southwest is 14 kilometres. The longest walk since the Kilo mission. Kilo was 56 kilometres over 4 days and we carried water. This is 28 kilometres over 5 days and we carry hope. Hope is lighter. Hope is also harder to set down. I checked the rifle. I checked the flares. I checked the ammunition. I will check them again in the morning. The checking is the thing I can do. The rest is the walk.

Three of my students are absent tomorrow. The Courier, the Hunter, and the Child Soldier is not absent but the Child Soldier is not a student tomorrow, he is a boy who is waiting. I do not know how to teach when the room is missing people. The Naive Son asked where the Courier was. I said the Courier is on a mission. He said, 'Again?' I said yes. He said, 'Does he come back?' I said yes. I said it the way you say a thing you cannot promise. The Naive Son is 16 and he hears the thing you cannot promise. He did not ask again. The Feral Orphan did not ask. The Feral Orphan does not ask where people go. The Feral Orphan knows where people go. Some of them do not come back. I will teach tomorrow. I will teach the water cycle again because the water cycle is the lesson that does not require anyone to be present. The water cycle is always happening. The water cycle does not know who is in the room. I wish I was the water cycle. I will teach the water cycle and I will leave a chair empty for the Courier and I will not say why the chair is empty because the Feral Orphan knows why and the Naive Son knows why and saying it would make it heavier and the water cycle is light. The water cycle is the lightest thing I know.

The compass oil from the fire lookout (exp_report_fire_lookout_01) is in the bunker clock escapement now. I cleaned the escapement, flushed the old oil — which had become a gum that was slowing the tick by an estimated 4 seconds per hour — and re-oiled with the compass oil. The clock is running. I timed it against the mechanical chronometer from the comms room. The discrepancy is now under 1 second per hour. This is the first time the bunker clock has been within 1 second since Day 40. The Chef came to the corridor to listen. She said the clock sounds different. I asked how. She said, 'It sounds like it knows what time it is.' I told her the clock does not know what time it is. The clock knows what speed it is. Time is the thing we agree to believe. She said, 'Then I agree to believe it.' She went back to the kitchen. The clock ticks. The compass oil is good oil. I have enough for one more service. After that, the clock will drift again, and I will calibrate it against the chronometer and post the correction, and the Chef will be annoyed, and the bread will not know. The bread does not know what time it is. The clock does not know what time it is. We agree to believe. That is what a clock is for.

The dormitory is missing three sounds tonight. The Courier is not here — he is on the warehouse walk. The Hunter is not here — he is with the Courier. The Exhausted Father is here but his daughter's cough is not, because the Surgeon says the dust has cleared and the cough is better, and the absence of a cough is a different kind of absence. I have learned the breathing of seven people. Tonight it is five and the two missing are the ones I did not realise I had learned until they were gone. The Bouncer still calls out his sister's name. I know it is his sister now. The Therapist did not tell me. The Bouncer told me, on Day 180, in the mess hall, without anyone asking. He said, 'The name is my sister. I say it in my sleep. I do not remember saying it.' I said, 'I know. I listen.' He looked at me and I looked at him and we did not say anything else. That is the kind of knowing the bunker is full of now. The knowing that does not need the words. The dormitory is missing three sounds and the three sounds are the Courier's breathing and the Hunter's breathing and the Exhausted Father's daughter's cough, and I did not know I had learned them until the room was different. I will know when they are back. The room will be different again. The different is how I know.

We are at the ridge. Day 1. 14 kilometres. The Veteran walks like he has walked 14 kilometres before, which he has, many times, in a life before this one that he does not talk about. The Mechanic walks like a man carrying a pry bar, which he is. The Hunter walks like a man who is listening to everything, which he is. I walk like a man carrying the Surgeon's list on his hand. I washed the hand at the stream crossing and the names blurred and I re-wrote them at the ridge with the pencil the Teacher gave the Child Soldier, which I borrowed, which I will return. Amoxicillin. Doxycycline. Ciprofloxacin. The names are on my hand and the hand is mine and the list is the Surgeon's and the Surgeon's hands shook when he wrote it. I did not tell him I saw. I will not tell him. The ridge is cold. We will not make a fire. The Hunter says fire is a beacon. The Veteran says fire is a beacon. The Mechanic says fire is warm. The Mechanic is outvoted. We sleep cold. I have the hand-crank radio. I will listen to 149.0 before I sleep. If the bunker is there, I will hear the carrier. If the bunker is there, they will hear nothing, because I am not transmitting. I am listening. Listening is the thing I can do from the ridge. The warehouse is tomorrow. The Surgeon's list is on my hand. The hand is steady. The hands that wrote it were not. I will be the steady hand for him. That is the job the Surgeon gave me. I did not know that was the job until I wrote it here.

The bulb is flickering. I am writing this in the greenhouse at 06:00 with the light on and the light is not steady. It is a small flicker — a half-second dim, then bright, then dim. A bulb that flickers is a bulb that is dying. I have known this since the first greenhouse I worked in, which was not this one, which had lights that did not flicker, which had a power grid, which had a world. The flicker is in the filament or the ballast or the connection and I do not know which and it does not matter which because the bulb is the last one and there is no second one and the LED retrofit the Electrician built is 5 percent and 5 percent is not a greenhouse. 5 percent is a candle. The wheat seedlings are on bed B under the flickering bulb. The barley is on bed B under the flickering bulb. I put them on the same bed because I will not split a dying light between two beds. They share it or they lose it together. That is the decision I made at 05:00. The Teacher would say it is a metaphor. It is not a metaphor. It is a bulb. I am a botanist. I grow things under lights. The light is dying. I will not pretend the light is not dying. I will document the flicker. I will document the hours the bulb holds. I will document the moment it fails. And then I will move the wheat seedlings to the LED array and I will watch them survive at 5 percent, which is not thriving, which is surviving, which is the thing the wheat does because the wheat is the proof and the proof outlives the practice. Suki said that. I said it to the council. I said I can accept it. I did not say I accept it gracefully. I do not accept it gracefully. I accept it the way a person accepts a season turning. The season is turning. The bulb is flickering. I am writing it down.

The number is 304. I wrote the viability report today and the number is 304 and the number is real. I did the solubility proxy on the amoxicillin and the solution was clear and the compound is intact and the expiry dates are 14 to 22 months in the future, which means the warehouse stock was not expired, which means it was produced for a distribution cycle that never completed, which means the world ended in the middle of someone's work and the work is still good. The work is still good. That is the sentence I keep coming back to. The Surgeon read the report and said, 'It is real. It is all real.' He said the same thing at the airlock. He is saying it again because the confirmation is the thing. I gave him the confirmation. I am not a doctor. I am a chemist. I test things. I tested the diesel and it was a breath. I tested the antibiotics and they are a future. The breath runs out on Day 195. The future runs out in 6 to 12 months. The breath and the future are different kinds of time and I have given the bunker both and I do not know if that is enough. I know it is not zero. I have written 'not zero' in three reports now. The diesel was not zero. The antibiotics are not zero. The grow light bulbs are zero. That is the next number. That is the number the Electrician and the Mechanic and the Courier and the Hunter are going to walk 12 kilometres to change. I am not going. I am staying with the lab. The lab is the place where the numbers are. The field is the place where the numbers come from. I am the number person. They are the number-getters. The number we need next is a bulb. The number is currently zero. I hope it is not zero when they come back.

The reserve is in the clinic. I counted it twice. 84 amoxicillin. 120 doxycycline. 60 ciprofloxacin. 40 metronidazole. 304. The Chemist's report says viable. The packaging says 14 to 22 months. The storage says pharmaceutical-grade. I have an antibiotic reserve. I have not had an antibiotic reserve in 146 days. For 146 days I have been a surgeon without antibiotics, which is a surgeon without the thing that makes surgery survivable, which is a surgeon who sews and prays. I do not pray. The Priest prays. I sew. Now I have the thing. I have it in a locked cabinet in the clinic. I have the key. I will not dispense a dose without my direct authorisation. That is the conservation protocol. I told the council. I told the Therapist. The Therapist asked me what it felt like to have the reserve. I said it feels like holding a breath. She said, 'You are the man who said the waiting cannot be taught. Can the holding be taught?' I said no. She said, 'Then you are learning it.' I am learning it. The holding is the thing you do with a finite resource that you cannot replace. The holding is the thing I did not have to learn for 146 days because there was nothing to hold. Now there is. The holding is harder than the not-having. I did not expect that. I will write it down because the page does not expect things of me. The holding is harder than the not-having. The not-having was a flat line. The holding is a line that goes down. I will hold it as long as I can. I will dispense when I must. I will document every dose. The reserve is 304. The reserve is real. The reserve is mine to hold.

I wrote the bulb guide today for the Courier and the Mechanic. The guide is: look for a tube, not a bulb. Look for T5 or T8 fluorescent tubes, 18 watts or 36 watts, 54 centimetres or 120 centimetres. Look for the bi-pin connector at both ends. Look for the manufacturer label. Do not take a tube that is blackened at the ends — that is a tube that has failed. Do not take a tube that is cracked. Take tubes that are in sealed sleeves or boxes. Take as many as you can carry. The ballasts are the other thing. A tube needs a ballast. Our fixtures have ballasts. If the ballasts are the failure, not the tubes, then the tubes we have are fine and the ballasts are the problem. I do not know if the ballasts are the problem. The flicker on bed B could be the tube or the ballast. I cannot test the ballast without a working tube to swap in. I have one working tube and it is the one that is flickering. If I swap it out to test the ballast, I lose the light. I will not lose the light to test the ballast. The guide says: take tubes and take ballasts if you find them. The ballasts are small metal boxes with two wires. I drew a picture. The Mechanic will know the box. The Courier will know the picture. The picture is a rectangle with two lines coming out. That is a ballast. I have done what I can. The rest is the walk and the finding. I am an electrician. I make things work. I cannot make a bulb that does not exist. I am going on the expedition because I am the one who knows the bulb. The General said the Electrician goes. I said the Electrician goes. The Electrician is me. I am going. I will leave the LED array on the wheat. The Botanist will watch it. The LED is 5 percent. The wheat will survive. The wheat is the proof. I am the practice. The practice is going to find a bulb.

The constraints reordered today. I did not reorder them. The reorder happened the way a season happens — not by decision but by the movement of the things themselves. The antibiotics are addressed. The fuel is counting down. The grow light is flickering. The flickering one is the one we can do something about. So the flickering one is the primary. I have learned that the primary constraint is not the most important one. It is the most movable one. The fuel is not movable. It is what it is. The antibiotics were movable and we moved them. The grow light is movable if the agri depot has bulbs. If it does not, the grow light becomes the fuel — a thing that is what it is. I told the Therapist this on Day 179. She said the body is kinder than the man. I am learning what she meant. The body responds to the number on the board. The number on the fuel board went up and I slept. The number on the grow light board is going down and I will not sleep tonight. The body is kinder because the body believes the number. The man knows the number is a story we tell ourselves about how long we have. The Therapist said I am two things — the body and the man. I am learning that the general is a third thing. The general is the one who decides which number to believe. Tonight the number is a flicker. Tomorrow the number is a walk. I will believe the walk because the walk is the thing I can do. The rest is the season.

We go tomorrow for the bulbs. The Electrician drew me a picture. A rectangle with two lines. That is a ballast. A tube with two pins. That is the bulb. I have the picture on the back of the Surgeon's list hand, which is fading, which I re-wrote this morning because the Surgeon's list is the hand I write on and the bulb guide is the other hand. I am running out of hands. The Teacher would say that is a metaphor. The Teacher is not here. The Teacher is in the classroom teaching the water cycle to the ones who are here. I am here and I am going. The agri depot is 12 kilometres. The first time we went for the potassium and the fleece and the lime. This time we go for the light. The light is the thing that grows the food. The food is the thing that feeds the people. The people are the 47. The 47 are the reason. The reason is the thing I carry. I carry it in the containers and in the list and in the picture and in the hands that are running out of space. The Hunter says I talk too much in my head. He is right. He says the walk is the walk. I say the walk is the reason. He says same thing. I do not think it is the same thing. I think the walk is the walk and the reason is the reason and the reason is why the walk is worth it. He says that is the same thing said twice. He is 40 and I am 22 and he has walked more than me. I will listen. I will walk. I will carry the picture and the containers and the reason. The reason is the bulbs. The bulbs are the light. The light is the food. The food is the 47. Tomorrow.

The cliff has been moved. I wrote it in the ledger today and I wrote it because the Botanist's light came on and the light does not flicker and the cliff that was 3 to 7 days is now a shelf that is 18 to 24 months. The shelf holds. The reserve holds. The countdown runs. I have been keeping the ledger for 160 days and the ledger has been a document of things going down. The rice goes down. The beans go down. the canned goods go down. The fuel goes down. Today, for the first time, the ledger has a thing that went up. The grow light reserve went from 0 tubes to 12 tubes. The shelf went from 3 to 7 days to 18 to 24 months. I wrote the number and I wrote 'shelf' and I wrote 'holds' and I looked at the word 'holds' and I did not know what to do with it. The ledger is full of words like 'declining' and 'critical' and 'ceiling' and 'countdown.' The word 'holds' does not fit. The word 'holds' is a word that stays. I wrote it. I left it. The reserve holds. The shelf holds. The countdown runs. The countdown is the only one that moves. The countdown is the fuel. The fuel is 13 days. I have been asked to find a second fuel source by Day 200. I have the Cartographer's map and the fire finder map and two candidates and one of them is too hot and the other is 18 kilometres away. 18 kilometres is the edge of the walkable range. 18 kilometres is the edge of the breath. I will find the fuel or I will write the day the fuel runs out and I will write '0' and I will write 'ceiling' and the ceiling will be the day the bunker learns to live without the generator. I am the Quartermaster. I count the things. The things are a reserve that holds, a shelf that holds, and a countdown that runs. The countdown is the one I watch. The countdown is the one that does not hold. That is the job.

I said 'we' today. I did not notice. The Therapist noticed. She said it was the healthiest thing I have said. I did not know I had said it. I said 'we move' in the council and I did not know I had stopped saying 'I move.' The Therapist says the 'we' is the integration. She says the body and the man are becoming the bunker. I do not know what that means. I know what it feels like. It feels like the decision is no longer mine. It is ours. That is either a relief or a surrender and I do not know which. The load-shed schedule is written. The Electrician wrote it. I signed it. The schedule says what the bunker will do without. The schedule is the will. The will is not for the man who writes it. The will is for the people who survive him. I said that to the Therapist and she did not say anything for a long time. Then she said, 'The bunker is the man who dies.' I said, 'Yes.' She said, 'And you are the man who signs.' I said, 'Yes.' She said, 'The signing is the living.' I did not understand. I understand now, writing it. The signing is the living because the signing is the thing I do while the bunker is the thing that dies. I sign. The bunker dies. I sign. That is the living. That is the 'we.'

I went. I went under the sky. The sky was very large and very grey and very close and I went under it. The General said I could stay at the perimeter. I stayed at the perimeter for 2 hours. The perimeter is the edge of the sky. The sky is above the perimeter and the perimeter is the last place the bunker is and the sky is the first place the bunker is not. I stood at the edge and the sky was above me and I could not breathe and I breathed. I breathed because the Mechanic needed the assessment and the assessment was the thing I could do and the thing I could do was inside the plant and the plant was under the sky and I went. I went under the sky and into the plant and the sky was above me the whole time and I did not look up. I did not look up because the sky is the thing I do not look at. I looked at the diesel. I looked at the maintenance shed. I looked at the fuel assessment. I did the work. The work was the thing that was not the sky. The Mechanic said, 'You are here.' I said, 'I am here.' He said, 'Good.' He did not say I was brave. He said I was here. That was the permission. The General gave me permission to be afraid. The Mechanic gave me permission to be useful. I needed both. I went. I came back. The sky is still large. I am still small. But I went. I told the Therapist. She said the fear is still there and I functioned alongside it. She said that is the definition of courage that is not the absence of fear but the functioning alongside it. I do not know if it was courage. I know it was the work. The work was under the sky. I did the work. I did not look up.

The light holds. The new tube has been on for 2 days and it does not flicker. The barley is under it. The wheat is under it. The LED array is off — I turned it off when the new tube came on (courier_mission_b2_022). The LED is the standby now. The new tube is the present. I check the tube every morning at 06:00. I look at the ends. The ends are not blackened. The ends are clean. A tube with clean ends is a tube that is not dying. I will check the ends every morning until the ends blacken or until I stop checking, which will be the day I stop being afraid, which will be the day the shelf runs out, which is 18 to 24 months, which is not tomorrow. Tomorrow the ends will be clean. I will check. The Therapist said the proof does not require an audience but the botanist does. She is right. I am the audience. I watch the wheat. I watch the tube. I watch the ends. The watching is the thing I do. The watching is the thing the Therapist said to come back if the light did not come on. The light came on. I came back anyway. I came back because the botanist requires an audience either way. The light holds. The ends are clean. I will check tomorrow.

The cabinet is locked. I have the key. The key is in my pocket. I have checked the key 7 times today. The Therapist would say that is a compulsion. I say it is the holding. The holding is the thing I do with the key. The key is the thing that opens the cabinet that holds the 304. The 304 is the reserve. The reserve holds. The key is in my pocket. I checked it 7 times. The 7th time I checked it I left it in my pocket and I did not check it again and I came to the journal because the journal is the thing that does not ask me to check. The journal asks me to write. I will write the number. 304. I will write the word. Holds. I will write the thing I do not say to the bunker. The thing I do not say is that the 304 is finite and the finite is the thing that makes it precious and the precious is the thing that makes the holding harder. The Therapist said the holding is harder than the not-having. She is right. The not-having was a flat line. The holding is a line that goes down. The line goes down slowly. The line goes down at the rate of infection. The rate of infection is low. The rate of infection is low because the water is clean and the kitchen is clean and the Chef washes his hands and the Plumber treats the water and the Chemist tests the water and the water is the thing that keeps the 304 from going down. The water is the thing that holds the holding. I will write that. The water holds the holding. The Plumber does not know that. I will tell him tomorrow. He will say something about pipes. He is right. The pipes are the thing that holds the water that holds the holding. The pipes and the 304 and the key in my pocket that I checked 7 times. The key is in my pocket. I will not check it again tonight.

The last breath. That is what the General called the municipal fuel depot. The last breath. I have carried breaths before. The diesel was a breath — 3 days on my back. The antibiotics were not a breath — they were a future, 18 kilograms, and I carried them and the Surgeon's hands were steady. The grow light tubes were a light — 12 tubes, glass, fragile, and I carried them like they were the 47. The last breath is 18 kilometres. 18 kilometres is the edge of the walkable range. 18 kilometres is the farthest I have walked. The Kilo mission was 56 kilometres over 4 days but it was 14 kilometres per day. The municipal depot is 18 kilometres out and 18 kilometres back and 36 kilometres in 3 days and 36 kilometres is the farthest. I will carry the fuel if there is fuel. I will carry the empty containers if there is not. The General said the last breath is the one that determines whether the bunker breathes or learns to live without breathing. I do not know what living without breathing looks like. I know what carrying looks like. I will carry. The fuel is heavy. The diesel is 0.84 kilograms per litre. If we find 50 litres, that is 42 kilograms. 42 kilograms is the weight of a child. I have not carried a child. I have carried water and antibiotics and tubes and a list on my hand. I will carry the fuel. The fuel is the last breath. The last breath is the heaviest. I will carry it because I am the Courier and the Courier carries and the carrying is the reason and the reason is the 47 and the 47 are the people and the people are the bunker and the bunker is the thing that breathes. I will carry the breath.

I saw it. The thing that watches the wolves. I saw it on Day 202 from 700 metres on the southwestern ridge. It was a figure. Human-shaped. Stationary. It did not move for the 40 minutes I watched. It watched the wolves. The wolves were on the ridge below it, 9 animals, the same pack, the same route. The figure was above the wolves. The figure watched the wolves the way I watch the deer. The way a person watches a thing they are assessing. The Cop saw it on Day 201. I saw it on Day 202. The Veteran saw it on Day 201 and Day 202. The Bouncer said it first. The Bouncer said it on Day 193 and we did not believe him and he was right. The Therapist said the Bouncer is not broken. The Bouncer is sharp. I am sharp too. I have been sharp since the first wolf track. The figure is a person who watches wolves. A person who watches wolves is a person who is learning the wolves. A person who is learning the wolves is a person who is either hunting the wolves or hunting with the wolves or hunting the thing the wolves hunt. The wolves hunt the deer. The figure watches the wolves hunt the deer. The figure is learning the deer. A person who learns the deer is a person who eats the deer. A person who eats the deer is a person who is near the bunker. A person who is near the bunker is a person the bunker must know. I told the General. The General said the southwestern ridge is restricted. I said the restriction does not make the figure go away. The General said he knows. I said the figure is learning us. The General said he knows. I said the figure was watching the wolves and the wolves are watching the deer and the deer are near the bunker and the figure is near the bunker. The General said he knows. He said the last breath is the fuel and the figure is the thing after the fuel. I said I do not understand. He said the fuel is the thing that runs out and the figure is the thing that arrives. I said the figure is already here. He said he knows. He said he knows 3 times. I stopped talking. I will watch the figure. I am the Hunter. I watch the things. The figure is the thing I watch now.

The schedule is posted. I posted it in the generator housing next to the fuel gauge. The schedule is the load-shed. The schedule says what runs and what does not and when. I wrote it in 2-day decrements because 2 days is the unit of the bunker. The council meets every 2 days. The expeditions go for 2 days. The breaths are 2 days. I wrote the schedule in the units the bunker thinks in. The schedule is not a plan. The schedule is a list of the things the bunker will do without. The first thing the bunker will do without is the mess hall and the laundry. The bunker has already done without the laundry. The Widow's towels are the laundry now. The second thing is the corridor heat. The lower corridor will be 8 degrees. The cast-iron stove is the fallback. The third thing is the grow lights. The LED is the fallback. The wheat survives. The barley does not. The fourth thing is the radio. The hand-crank is the fallback. The bunker listens. The bunker does not speak. The last thing is the medical cold storage and the ventilation. The ventilation goes manual. The cold storage goes passive. The 304 goes to the lower corridor. The schedule is the document that says the bunker will do without and the doing without is the living. I wrote it. I posted it. I stood in the generator housing and I looked at the fuel gauge and the fuel gauge said 135 litres and the schedule said 13 days and I stood there and I did not write a schedule for the day after the 13 days because the schedule does not go past the generator. The schedule is the generator. The generator is the schedule. When the generator stops, the schedule stops, and the bunker does what the schedule said and the doing is the living and the living is the doing without. I am the Electrician. I make things work. I wrote the schedule for the things that will not work. That is the work.

The chairs are empty again. The Courier is on the last breath walk. The Hunter is with him. The Electrician is with him. The Mechanic is with him. Four chairs empty. The Naive Son is here. The Feral Orphan is here. The Child Soldier is here. The bunker-born children are here. Six students and four empty chairs. I taught the water cycle again. I have taught the water cycle 14 times. The water cycle is the lesson that does not require anyone to be present. The water cycle is always happening. Today I taught it differently. I said: the water cycle does not know who is in the room. The water cycle does not know if the chairs are empty. The water cycle does not know if the people are coming back. The water cycle happens anyway. The Feral Orphan said, 'Like the light.' I said, 'Like the light.' The Naive Son said, 'The light is a tube. The water cycle is a cycle. They are not the same.' I said, 'They are the same in the way that matters. They happen whether we watch or not.' The Naive Son thought about this. He said, 'That is the thing my mother would have said.' He did not say 'is' this time. He said 'would have.' The tense changed. I did not say anything. The tense change is the thing the Therapist would note. I am not the Therapist. I am the Teacher. I teach the water cycle. The tense changed and the water cycle did not change and the chairs are empty and the water cycle happens anyway and the light is on and the light does not flicker and the Feral Orphan said 'like the light' and the Naive Son said 'would have' and the Child Soldier wrote the word for water in his book and the pencil is yellow and the water cycle happens anyway.

The chapel filled today. I did not expect it. I have been keeping the chapel for 160 days. Six chairs and a table. For the last 3 weeks, no one came. I sat alone. I said the words I remember. I did not know if I remembered them correctly. Today, 4 people came. The Widow came. The Exhausted Father came. The Historian came. The Child Soldier came. The Child Soldier brought his yellow pencil. He did not write. He held it. The Widow sat in the chair nearest the door. The Exhausted Father sat in the chair nearest the wall. The Historian sat in the middle. I did not ask why they came. I said the words I remember. I said them the way I always say them — not certain I remember them correctly, not certain they are the right words, certain only that they are the words I have. The Child Soldier held his pencil. The Widow folded her hands. The Exhausted Father closed his eyes. The Historian listened. I do not know what the Historian heard. The Historian is the bunker's memory and the memory heard the words I remember and the memory will remember them differently than I said them and that is what memories do. I said the words. Four people came. The chapel filled. It was not full. It was filled. The filling is the thing. The filling is the thing that happened after 3 weeks of empty. I do not know if they will come back. I know they came. The chapel is 6 chairs and a table and 4 people and a yellow pencil and the words I remember. That is enough. It has to be.

I met the Cartographer. I sat at the cache and I waited and he came. He came the way the Hunter comes — watching before moving, moving only when he had watched. He set the distance at 4 metres. I did not stand. I offered the gifts before the questions. He took the mushrooms and the salt and the grow light tube and the map. He took the antibiotics last. His hands shook when he took the antibiotics. I did not say anything. The Surgeon's hands shook when he wrote the list (journal_raw_b3_17). The Cartographer's hands shook when he took the gift. The shaking is the thing that is the same in both men and the shaking is the thing that means the antibiotics are not a number. The antibiotics are a thing that makes hands shake. I gave him the 5 doses and his hands shook and I knew the 5 doses were the right thing to give because the giving is the thing that costs the giver and the receiver the same thing — the knowledge that the 5 are finite and the finite is the thing that is precious. He answered the questions. He spoke in long sentences with pauses. He said the wolves are a map. He said the spring is coming. He said the moss is the first. He said the bunker is a staying settlement that walks and that is rare. He said he needs the bunker to continue. He said the seeds need a place and the bunker is the place. He said plant the seeds. I will plant the seeds. I carried the bunker to the Cartographer and I carried the Cartographer's maps and seeds back to the bunker. The heaviest thing I have carried is not the fuel. The fuel was 67 kilograms. The relationship is heavier. The relationship does not fit in a container. It fit in the 3 hours. The 3 hours are the thing I carry now. The 3 hours are the heaviest and the lightest thing because the 3 hours are the thing that does not weigh anything and the thing that weighs everything. The Cartographer is the thing I am, outside the bunker. I am the thing the Cartographer is, inside the bunker. We are the same thing in different places. That is the relationship. That is the thing I wrote in the journal because the journal does not ask me to explain it. The relationship does not need explaining. The relationship is.

The counting up. The Therapist said it is the thing she has been waiting to hear. I did not know I was going to say it. The depot made me say it. The depot is the thing that made the counting turn. The counting down was the thing I did for 175 days. The counting down is the thing the Quartermaster does. The Quartermaster does not know how to count up. The Quartermaster will learn. The bunker will learn. The counting up is the days until the spring. The days until the planting. The days until the food is on the surface and the greenhouse is a bridge and not a destination. The days until the bunker is not a bunker. The days until the bunker is a place. The bunker will always be a bunker. The bunker will also be a place. A bunker is a thing you survive in. A place is a thing you live in. The spring is the thing that turns the bunker into a place. The Cartographer said the spring is coming. The Cartographer said the moss is the first. The moss is the thing that grows when the ground remembers how to grow. The ground is remembering. The bunker is remembering. The counting up is the thing the bunker does when it is not counting down. The counting up is the thing I do now. I am the General. I am the man who counts up. I did not know I was the man who counts up. I know it now. The depot made me say it. The spring makes me know it.

The seeds. The Cartographer gave the bunker 10 varieties of heirloom seeds. I opened the packet in the greenhouse at 06:00 and I held them in my hand and I counted them. 10 varieties. Wheat (2 varieties — the Cartographer does not know the names, only that they are wheat), barley, rye, oats, peas, beans, lentils, radish, and a leafy green I do not recognise. The seeds are the Cartographer's cache stock. The seeds have been in the packet for an unknown time. I will test viability with the germination test — 10 seeds of each variety on wet paper, 7 days, count the sprouts. If the germination is above 50 percent, the seeds are plantable. The Cartographer said plant the seeds. The Cartographer said the seeds need a place and the bunker is the place. The seeds are the spring. The spring is the thing that moves the food from the greenhouse to the surface. The greenhouse is the bridge. The surface is the destination. The seeds are the thing that crosses the bridge. I held the seeds in my hand and I thought of Tomas. Tomas would have calculated the probability. I did not calculate. I held. The holding is the thing the Surgeon does with the 304. The holding is the thing I do with the seeds. The 304 are the holding that is a reserve. The seeds are the holding that is a future. The future is the thing that grows. The growing is the thing that happens when the ground remembers. The ground is remembering. The seeds are the thing I will plant when the ground says yes. The ground will say yes by Day 250. The seeds are ready. I am ready. The greenhouse is the bridge. The surface is the destination. The seeds are the crossing.

The data is confirming. Barometric pressure: rising for 21 days. Wind: southwest for 14 days. Particulate density: down 35 percent since Day 180. Surface dose in the low-dose zones: 1.8 uSv/h average (down from 3.2 uSv/h on Day 180). The trend is consistent. The trend is not a single day. The trend is 3 weeks. 3 weeks is a season turning. The season is turning from winter to spring. The spring is the thing the Cartographer said is coming. The data says the Cartographer is right. The data says the Cartographer is right the way the Chemist says the diesel is generator-grade — the data confirms what the observer observed. The Cartographer observed the moss. I observed the pressure. The moss and the pressure are the same thing in different instruments. The moss is the Cartographer's instrument. The pressure is mine. The Cartographer reads the moss. I read the barometer. We are both reading the spring. The spring is the thing that does not ask to be read. The spring happens. The reading is the thing we do to be ready. The planting window is Day 250-260. I will confirm by Day 245. The confirmation is the thing the Botanist needs. The Botanist has the seeds. The seeds need the ground. The ground needs the spring. The spring needs the data. The data is mine. I am the Meteorologist. I read the sky. The sky is the thing the Chemist does not look at. I look at it for her. The sky is the thing that tells me the spring. The spring is coming. The data says so.

I am cross-referencing the Cartographer's maps with the bunker's existing maps. The Cartographer's maps are more detailed than the fire finder map (exp_report_fire_lookout_01) and cover the areas the bunker has not explored. The fuel and water map shows 2 additional water sources and 1 additional fuel source (a heating oil depot 22km north). The low-dose zone map shows 4 zones within 20km. The settlement map shows 6 settlements within 50km. I am cross-referencing the settlement map with the arrival list (journal_raw_b3_03). 3 of the 6 settlements are unknown to the bunker — the bunker has not encountered them in 225 days. The 3 unknown settlements are the thing the bunker does not know. The not-knowing is the thing the bunker has lived with for 225 days. The not-knowing is the thing the Cartographer's maps reduce. The maps do not remove the not-knowing. The maps reduce it. The reducing is the thing the Historian does. I keep the list of the living. I keep the maps of the known. The living and the known are the things the bunker has. The not-known and the not-living are the things the bunker does not have. The Cartographer's maps move 3 settlements from the not-known to the known. That is the thing the maps do. The maps move things from the not-known to the known. That is the thing the Historian does. I am the Historian. I keep the known. The Cartographer is the thing that expands the known. The Cartographer and the Historian are the same thing in different places. The Cartographer walks the unknown and maps it. The Historian keeps the known and records it. The maps are the thing that connects us. I will cross-reference the maps and I will write the expanded known and I will give it to the council. The known is the thing the bunker has. The known is growing. The growing is the counting up.

The source. I have been keeping the ledger for 226 days and the ledger has been a document of things going down. Today the ledger has a thing that goes up. The fuel is a source. The source is the thing that does not go down. The source is the thing that stays. I wrote 'source' in the ledger. I wrote it next to the fuel line. The fuel line used to say 'ceiling' and 'countdown' and 'days remaining.' The fuel line now says 'source' and 'standing trip' and 'days of supply (source).' The days of supply from the source are 82 days (820 litres at 10L/day) plus the 155 litres in the reserve (15 days). The total is 97 days of fuel. 97 days is not a breath. 97 days is a season. 97 days is the winter ending and the spring beginning and the spring is the thing that makes the greenhouse a bridge. The fuel is the thing that powers the bridge. The source is the thing that powers the fuel. The depot is the source. The depot is 18km. The depot is the farthest thing the bunker walks to, and the farthest thing is now a habit. The habit is the standing trip. The standing trip is the thing that does not ask permission. I am grateful for the habit. I am grateful for the source. I am grateful for the word 'source' in the ledger. The word 'source' is the word that stays. The word 'ceiling' is the word that falls. The word 'countdown' is the word that runs. The word 'source' is the word that stays. I wrote it. I left it. The source holds.

The Botanist let me hold the seeds. She said I could hold them if I was careful. I was careful. The seeds are small. Some are round and some are long and some are flat. They do not look like the thing that grows. They look like the thing that is small. The Botanist said the small thing is the thing that grows. I said how does the small thing know to grow. She said the small thing does not know. The small thing grows when the ground is warm and the water is there and the light is there. The small thing does not know. The small thing grows. I said that is like the pencil. She said what is the pencil. I said the pencil does not know the words. The pencil writes the words when the hand moves. She said yes. She said the seeds are the pencil and the ground is the hand and the spring is the hand moving. I said the spring is the hand. She said yes. I held the seeds and I thought of the pencil. The pencil is yellow. The seeds are brown and green and tan. The seeds are not yellow. The seeds are the thing that grows when the hand moves. The spring is the hand. I will watch the seeds grow. I will write the word for seed in my book. The word for seed is the next word. The Teacher will teach me. The pencil will write it. The seeds will grow it. The spring will move the hand.

The towels are by the stove now. I moved them when the corridor went cold (maint_log_b3_019). The laundry alcove is empty. The alcove was the nest and the nest is empty and the towels are by the stove and the stove is the thing that is warm. The Widow is the thing that moves toward the warm. I have been the thing that moves toward the warm since the dormitory. The dormitory is warm. The corridor was cold. The stove is warm. The towels are by the stove. The towels are not a nest. The towels are towels. I fold them by the stove because the folding is the thing I do. The folding is the thing the Therapist said is a habit and the habit is the thing that does not ask permission. I fold the towels by the stove. The Bouncer sits by the stove in the evening. He does not speak. I do not speak. We sit by the stove and the towels are between us and the stove is warm and the not-speaking is the knowing. The Bouncer named his sister to me on Day 180. I have not told anyone. The Bouncer is the thing that sits by the stove and does not speak and the not-speaking is the thing that holds the name. The name is the thing between us. The towels are the thing between us. The stove is the thing between us. The between is the thing that is the knowing. The spring is coming. The corridor will be warm again. The towels will go back to the alcove. The alcove will be the place I was. The stove will be the place I am. The spring will be the place I go. I do not know where I go. I know I go toward the warm.

The spring is coming. The Cartographer said it. The Meteorologist confirmed it. The Botanist has the seeds. The spring is the thing the chapel has been waiting for. The chapel filled on Day 203 (journal_raw_b3_38) with 4 people. The chapel has had 4 people every Wednesday and every Sunday since. The 4 are the Widow, the Exhausted Father, the Historian, and the Child Soldier. The Child Soldier brings the yellow pencil. The Exhausted Father closes his eyes. The Historian listens. The Teacher said I said 'would have' instead of 'is' (journal_raw_b3_37). I did not know I said it. The Teacher said the tense changed. The Therapist would say the tense change is the thing. The past is the thing that is gone. The not-here is the thing that is not gone and not here. The not-here is the thing that is the not-knowing. The not-knowing is the thing the Therapist called ambiguous loss (therapy_session_b3_006). I did not know the word for it. I know the word now. Ambiguous loss. The loss that is not a loss because the person is not gone. The loss that is a loss because the person is not here. The ambiguous loss is the thing I have been carrying for 195 days. The ambiguous loss is the thing that the 'would have' is the tense of. The 'would have' is the tense that says the mother would have said the thing if the mother were here. The mother is not here. The mother is in the past. The 'would have' is the tense that knows the mother is in the past. The knowing is the thing that changed. The tense changed because the knowing changed. The knowing changed because the bunker changed. The bunker changed because the spring is coming. The spring is the thing that makes the knowing possible. The spring is the thing that makes the past the past and the not-here the not-here and the present the present. The present is the thing I am in. The present is the thing the bunker is in. The present is the thing the spring is in. I am in the present. The tense is in the present. The knowing is in the present.

The radish broke the surface. Day 257. 07:30. I knelt in the soil of zone 1 and the radish was there. Two leaves. Small. Green. Not the sickly yellow-green of the hydroponic trays. Green. The outdoor classroom began today. Day 265. Zone 1. The radish row. 6 students: the Naive Son, the Feral Orphan, the Child Soldier, the bunker-born children (2). The sixth student is the Bouncer. The walls are in the bunker. The surface does not have walls. The surface has the sky. The sky is the wall that is not a wall. The sky is the thing the learning is under.

I went to the surface. Day 267. The chapel went outside. I went outside. I have not been outside since I arrived. I do not know how many days it has been. The Historian would know. The Bouncer is the watcher. The Bouncer watched me look at the sky. The Bouncer did not speak. The Bouncer is the thing that watches the looking. I looked at the sky. The first lesson on the surface was the water cycle. The first lesson on the surface was the lesson that does not require anyone to be present (journal_raw_b3_19).
